title: Biography of the Seven Perfected Ones
excerpt: In all the world no task is hard to do; / the fear is but a heart resolved and true.

inline.s: (from The Seven Perfected Ones)
In all the world no task is hard to do; / the fear is but a heart resolved and true.

blocks.text: 1. Pitying Poverty, She Bestows a Small Kindness; Entering a Dream, He Points Out the Wandering Way

inline.s: Do good where good is truly done; / seek not vain fame beneath the sun;
What use is praise that is not true? / It only makes the poor cry out on you.

These few lines say that in doing good there must be solid substance. If one only seeks to make a fine show and wants people to know of it, that is buying empty fame. To have the name without the substance, to act only where things are lively and crowded, then the very poor and the very wretched who cannot be reached by one's bounty are many. Though one spends a great deal of silver and money, in the end one has never done any proper good deed. And having failed to do proper good, one may only sigh that it slipped by before one's eyes!

In the last years of the Yan Song (the Song dynasty), in Xianyang county of Shaanxi there was a village called Great Wei. In the village there were more than a hundred households, more than half of them surnamed Wang, so that it could be reckoned a great clan. In this Wang clan there was a widowed woman, over forty years of age. She had a son and a daughter, both of them already married. Because this widow was charitable by nature, when she saw other people's little boys and small girls she treated them as if they were her own, and was forever coaxing them with this and that. When those little ones cried they would call for their mama, and she would answer them offhand; and so everyone called her Mama Wang.

This Mama Wang's household was quite well off, and all her life she loved to do good deeds. She was fondest of the two paths of Buddhism and Daoism, and was always glad to feed monks and give alms to Daoists, to bow to the buddhas and read the scriptures. Everyone said she did good, and so many monks and Daoists came to her door to seek donations, and a good many poor folk came to the village to beg; more or less, she would relieve them as occasion offered. In the depths of that winter, when snow filled the sky, Mama Wang stood at her gate and saw two beggars come through the snow to seek her charity. Mama Wang scolded them: “Instead of hiring yourselves out to earn your daily bread, you come begging from door to door. If you are not gluttons who hate to work, then you are idlers greedy of ease. Where would I get so much spare tea and idle rice to wait upon the likes of you?” Before she had finished speaking, several monks and Daoists came to beg, and Mama Wang gave them money and rice. When the monks and Daoists had gone, the two beggars asked, “Good granny, you like to give to monks and Daoists but will not relieve the poor and the cold — why is that?” Mama Wang said, “It is not that I like to give to monks and Daoists. Monks can recite scriptures, Daoists can cultivate; though I give them a little money and rice, the monks can dispel calamity for me and the Daoists can lengthen my years. If I relieve you, what good does it do me? You only make a noise at my gate.” The two beggars said, “To bestow kindness and not look for reward — to look for reward is not to bestow kindness. Today you give us a bowl of rice and a few coins, and at once you want calamity dispelled and life lengthened; is that not absurd?” With that they went away.
To feed the monks and give alms is to weave good ties; / yet the poor and the lonely are pitiable in our eyes;
To give to monks and Daoists and pass the poor by / is to lose the first merit that good deeds can buy.

Now to continue. When the two beggars saw that Mama Wang would not relieve them, they had no choice but to go on their way. Before they had gone far they came to a gate-house of vermilion lacquer, and shouted aloud: “Grandfather, we beg your charity!” Presently a man came out from within. This man was ruddy of face and long of beard, of bright spirit and clear countenance, with a nature that could bear with others and the bearing of a gallant knight, and he was no more than forty years old. His surname was Wang and his given name Zhe (
zhé

, anciently the same as the character for “wise”), his style-name Zhiming, his sobriquet Desheng. In his youth he had read the Odes and the Documents, but success in the examinations was not his; so he cast aside letters and took up arms, and passed as head of the military examination, becoming a Filial and Incorrupt. On this day the sky sent down great snow and it was bitterly cold; he was sitting before the hall with his wife of the Zhou family, Madam Zhou, and his son Qiulang, gathered around the brazier to warm themselves, when suddenly he heard shouting at the gate, calling upon grandfather to relieve them. When the military graduate Wang heard these words, they struck him as very strange; he went out and saw two beggars standing at the gateway. The military graduate Wang asked them, “Which is it, in fact — that you beg grandfather for charity, or that grandfather begs for charity?” The beggars answered, “Words cannot be told in full; told in full, they must breed doubt.” The military graduate Wang saw that there was reason in his words, and asked no more.

At that time the wind was high and the snow thick, and the snow danced in the wind. Pear blossoms filled the sky and fell thick to the ground; the hills were cut off from bird tracks, the roads from human footsteps. Seeing that the two beggars had but a single layer of clothing, how could they withstand such bitter cold? A feeling of compassion suddenly rose in him, and he said to the two beggars, “Let us set aside those idle words. In such snow as this, how can you travel? At the side of my gate-house there is an empty room, and in it a heap of loose straw, where one may sit or lie down. Why do you not come in and shelter from the snow?” The two beggars answered, “That would be best.” The military graduate Wang at once opened the empty room, and the two beggars went in and settled themselves. The military graduate Wang went back to the hall and sent the servant boy Yuwa out with some food for the two beggars to eat.
How few are they who, brave and free, / will bid the poor come in and see?
In that year only Wang the bold / was generous, with a heart of gold.

Two days the two beggars lodged in the military graduate Wang's house, and only then did the sky clear; they thought to take their leave and go. Just then the military graduate Wang came in, with Yuwa following behind carrying wine and food. The military graduate said to the two beggars, “These past days I have had matters to attend to, and have been remiss in keeping you company. Today I am at leisure, and would like to drink a cup with you both and exchange a few words of greeting — what say you?” The two beggars cried that it would be excellent. The military graduate Wang at once called Yuwa to set out cups and chopsticks, and the two beggars, without any modest declining and without a word of thanks, fell to eating and in a moment emptied two pots between them. The military graduate Wang told Yuwa to bring more wine. While the two beggars drank deep, the military graduate Wang said, “What are the names of you two fellow-sufferers, and what trade have you followed in your lives?” The beggars answered, “We two can do nothing at all. His name is Jin Zhong, and mine is Wuxin Chang.” The military graduate Wang said, “I have a mind to put up a little capital for the two of you, so that you may do some small trade and live out your days; would that not be better than begging? I do not know what you two think of it.” No sooner had the military graduate finished speaking than Jin Zhong waved his hand and said, “No good, no good. All my life I have been used to a loose and careless life; I cannot do this business of having my hands and feet tied.” When the military graduate Wang heard Jin Zhong speak so, he knew he would not take up a trade. He asked Wuxin Chang again, “Since Brother Jin cannot do this small trade to live out his days, I wonder whether Brother Wu would be willing?” Wuxin Chang said, “My carelessness is greater still! I have heard it said: The yard-fowl has its food, and bides beside the pot; / the wild crane has no grain, yet flies high as it will. / If one must stoop for profit like a fly's head, / how could this body ever roam at ease?”

The military graduate Wang sighed and said, “From the words of you two, one may well see a lofty spirit. But the way of the world today is to prize caps and gowns (that is, the gentry and the scholar-officials) and to love silver and money; if you two are so plain and unassuming, who will ever know you?” Wuxin Chang said, “We are men who do not seek to be known. If we sought to be known, we would not have fallen to begging.” The military graduate Wang, hearing words so far above the common run, said no more; he told Yuwa to clear away the cups and dishes, and went in with him.

The next day the two beggars took their leave and rose to go. The military graduate Wang escorted them beyond the village, still reluctant to part. He walked a few steps further with them, when suddenly a bridge appeared, blocking the way. The military graduate Wang thought to himself that before and behind the village there had never been any bridge; he turned to look back at Great Wei Village, but it was faint and dim, not clearly to be made out. As he stood in doubt, Wuxin Chang called to him, “Come quickly, Master Filial and Incorrupt!” The military graduate Wang turned his head and saw the two of them sitting at the head of the bridge. Jin Zhong clapped his hands and sang:
Wealth gathers and scatters, and comes to naught; / the robe of office rots, as it ought. / Better by far are we than they / who stand within the world's own way.
We owe no grain to the state, / no debt to our children's fate; / we speak no good and we speak no ill, / nor of rise and fall say our fill.
We keep no company with the world, / and so no man's blame on us is hurled.
A single ragged coat have we, / worn on the body year by year; / torn, we patch it carefully; / washed, we dry it in sunlight clear.
By day it wraps the body's frame, / by night it serves as quilt the same; / no thief will come to steal it away, / no petty man will covet it, I say.
Ever we keep a soaring mind, / one heart to the higher realms inclined.
If a man our mind could know, / he would bow his head full low; / ours is a truth that has no end, / to keep him a thousand years on end.
Alas, men know us not, and so / our kindness turns to harm and woe.

The Filial and Incorrupt stepped quickly up onto the bridge, and Wuxin Chang said, “Since you have escorted us so far, Master Filial and Incorrupt, we owe you a cup of wine.” With that he took from his sleeve a small pewter bottle with a wine-cup over its mouth, poured from it, and it was full of fine wine; he handed it to the Filial and Incorrupt. The military graduate Wang took it in his hand and drained it at a draught; three cups in a row, and he was drunk and fell upon the bridge, drowsy and ready for sleep. Suddenly he saw Wuxin Chang come and pull him up with one hand, saying, “Do not sleep, do not sleep; come with us and look at the view.” The Filial and Incorrupt, fuddled with wine, followed Wuxin Chang a few steps, and saw a high mountain of the utmost steepness blocking the way. The Filial and Incorrupt said in alarm, “How shall we ever climb such a mountain as this?” Jin Zhong said, “Follow me, and you will rise of yourself.” The Filial and Incorrupt did indeed follow him and walked without the least effort. In a moment they were on the summit, which was very flat, and there was a great pool filled with clear water. In the water seven golden lotuses were in bloom, each flower as large as a platter, of rare freshness and beauty. The Filial and Incorrupt loved them greatly at heart and praised them again and again: “Fine lotuses! Fine lotuses! How can one be plucked and given to me?”

Before the Filial and Incorrupt had finished speaking, Wuxin Chang leaped into the pool and plucked all seven golden lotuses at once, and handed them to Wang the Filial and Incorrupt, saying, “I give them all to you; you must guard these seven golden lotuses well. They have seven masters: Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, Wang, and Sun. These seven have the bond of master and disciple with you; when you meet them in days to come, open and transform them well, and only then will you not have failed the meaning of my entrusting the lotuses to you.” The Filial and Incorrupt took the lotuses and clasped them to his breast, and at once wished to go home. As he was leaving he asked Wuxin Chang again, “When shall we meet again?” Wuxin Chang said, “Our meeting is not far away — / only two threes, and then the day. / Where we parted, there we meet; / by the bridge all ties are made complete.” When the Filial and Incorrupt had heard this, he moved his steps down the mountain. Suddenly he was tripped by a creeping vine beside the path and fell headlong down the mountain. Whether he lived or died, hear the next chapter's unfolding.
Say not that climbing up was hard; / know that coming down is harder far.

blocks.text: 2. At the Bridge of Ten Thousand Ties He Truly Transmits the Wondrous Way; in Great Wei Village He Feigns a Stroke

inline.s: Awakening is like finding a lamp in the night; / a windowless dark room is suddenly filled with light;
If in this life this body is not freed, / in what life then shall this body be freed indeed?

The story tells that Wang the Filial and Incorrupt, clasping the seven lotuses, moved his steps down the mountain, when suddenly a creeping vine tripped his foot and he fell headlong. He woke with a start, and all ten thousand things were empty: it had been a dream. When he opened his eyes he was lying in the study of his own house. He saw his son Qiulang standing at his side, and the Filial and Incorrupt gave a cough. Qiulang heard it and cried out, “Papa is awake! Papa is awake!” This cry roused Madam Zhou, who hurried in to ask after him, saying, “Has my husband waked from his wine?” The Filial and Incorrupt said, “How strange! How strange!” Madam Zhou said, “All things come of one's own delusion; what is there strange in it?” The Filial and Incorrupt said, “I plainly escorted my guests out of the house — why am I still at home?” Madam Zhou answered, “You are too wild altogether. Yesterday you went out to escort the two beggars and did not return for half a day. We sent people to look for you several times, but there was no trace of you. I could not set my mind at rest, so I begged your second uncle Wang Mao to go with Yuwa to find you. More than twenty li away they found you lying drunk upon a bridge, so fuddled with wine that you knew nothing at all, and they hired a cart to bring you home. You have slept a day and a night, and only now are you awake. From this day on, husband, you must take better care of yourself: drink less wine, do what is proper, and keep no company with men of doubtful origin. You have received the court's cap and rank, and are looked up to by the country people; if you lie drunk in the wild fields, what sort of conduct is that? Would you not lose your dignity and make yourself a laughing-stock to the villagers?”

The Filial and Incorrupt rose and thanked her, saying, “Wife, your words are good medicine; how dare I not engrave them on my heart? I believe those two fellow-sufferers of yesterday must have been two immortals.” Madam Zhou said, “They were plainly two beggars; how can you call them two immortals?” The Filial and Incorrupt said, “From their words and from their bearing I know that they must be immortals.” Madam Zhou asked, “What words did they speak? What did they do, that any part of it should look like an immortal?” Thereupon the Filial and Incorrupt told Madam Zhou the whole story from the beginning: how he had offered to put up capital for them, and how they had refused; how on the next day, after he had escorted them only a few steps, there had been more than twenty li of road; how they had sung their song; how they had given him wine; how they had gone up the mountain to gather lotuses; and all that they had said at parting. He added, “I drank but three cups of his wine, and was drunk for a day and a night. Such strange things as these — had they not been immortals, how could such wonders have happened?” Madam Zhou said, “I have heard tell that there are wicked men in this world who have the art of shrinking the earth, so that a single step carries them ten li away, and in one day they can travel a thousand li. They also put drugged powder into wine and carry it about with them. When they see a merchant traveling alone, they press the wine on him. No sooner does the wine touch his lips than he falls senseless; and they rob him of his silver and strip him of his clothes. By the time you wake, there is nowhere to look for them. If one is not careful beforehand, one must repent afterwards.” When Madam Zhou had finished, the Filial and Incorrupt thought to himself, “After all, my wife is a woman; if I argue with her, I shall never make the matter clear. Better to go along with her view and have done with it.” So he answered offhand, “What you say is right, wife; I shall certainly bear it in mind.”

Madam Zhou withdrew. The Filial and Incorrupt often sat alone in his study, thinking over the words of Jin Zhong and Wu Xinchang, turning them over and over and silently grasping their meaning. After many days he suddenly understood: “The two words Jin and Zhong, joined together, make the character Zhong. ‘Wu Xinchang’ is ‘Chang Without a Heart’; and the character Chang with the heart taken out of it makes the character Lü. Plainly it was the two immortals Zhongli and Lü who came to save me, and I, having no destiny for it, let them pass by before my very eyes!” The more he thought, the more it seemed so, and he could not keep from sighing aloud, “What a pity! What a pity!” Then he suddenly recalled their parting words: “Our meeting is not far away — only two threes; where we parted, there we meet; by the bridge all ties are made complete.” ‘Not far’ must mean that it would be soon. ‘Two threes’ must be the third day of the third month. ‘Where we parted, there we meet’: if one would know where they come from, one must seek it in the place where they went. ‘All ties are made complete’ speaks of all dharmas returning to one. When he had thought this far, joy rose in his heart without his knowing it. Time flies like an arrow, the sun and moon like a shuttle; in the twinkling of an eye the last of winter was gone and the new spring had come again.
Each year the year puts on a new face; / ten thousand flowers contend in another spring's grace;
The little children all are grown; / and soon the white-haired heads are shown.

Now when Wang the Filial and Incorrupt had passed the New Year, in the turn of an eye it was the third month. On the third day he slipped away from home and took the old road to the bridge. He waited a long while and no one came; he pondered their appearance in his mind, and his heart was most earnest and sincere. He stood at the head of the bridge, gazing east and west. Suddenly he heard someone behind him call, “Master Filial and Incorrupt, how early you have come!” The Filial and Incorrupt turned his head and saw that it was indeed the two fellow-sufferers of the year before. He hurried forward, caught them by the sleeve, and said, “You two great immortals, once gone, gave no thought to your poor disciple, I fear.” Wuxin Chang and Jin Zhong sat down at the head of the bridge. The Filial and Incorrupt knelt before them on both knees and said, “Your disciple Wang Zhe, with mortal eyes and a common body, did not know that high immortals had descended, and was often disrespectful; I beg you to pardon me. To see your immortal countenances again today is truly the good fortune of three lifetimes. I beg you to point out the erring path to me and let me mount the road of awakening; your disciple's gratitude would be deep.” Having spoken, he did nothing but knock his head on the ground. The two of them laughed heartily, and golden light flowed from their mouths, dazzling the eyes; and in the space of a bow and a lifting of the head, the two changed their appearance. The one on the left had his hair done in two topknots, wore an open robe, had a face like a ripe jujube, eyes like bright stars, a long beard hanging down over his breast, and a goose-feather fan in his hand. The one on the right wore a nine-ridged cap, a yellow Daoist robe, had a face like the full moon, eyes that pierced one through, and a sword girt at his side. They were in truth the Ancient Ancestor Zhongli and the Ancestor Lü Chunyang. The Filial and Incorrupt bowed low, not daring to raise his eyes.

The Ancestor Lü said, “In high antiquity men's hearts were plain and their customs good and honest; those who transmitted the Way first gave them the arts of magic to guard the body, and afterwards handed on the mysterious work of becoming true. In these times the world's way is thin and shallow, and men's hearts are not as of old; if one first gave them the arts of magic, it would only ruin them, and so we first transmit the mysterious work. Without borrowing magic the body is of itself at peace; without using transformations the Way of itself is accomplished. When the Way is accomplished, all dharmas are understood; without seeking magic, magic comes of itself. This is what is called the teaching of Quanzhen, the Complete Reality.” Then he spoke the wondrous principle of Complete Reality, saying:

What is called Complete Reality means pure truth without any admixture of the false. Who is without a true heart? But once it turns, it is no longer true. Who is without a true intent? But once it is mixed, it is lost. Who is without a true feeling? But once it leans aside, it goes astray. The first heart is true; when it changes and shifts, it becomes a false heart. The first intent is true; when it calculates and compares, it becomes a false intent. The utmost feeling is true; when it turns perverse, it becomes a false feeling. What is called the first heart is the heart that is already one's own; what is called the first intent is the intent at its first faint stirring; what is called the utmost feeling is the feeling of one's own nature. When the heart holds true intent and true feeling, then in the feeling one sees the true heart and true intent; from the true heart issues the true intent, and from the true intent issues the true feeling. This feeling is the very scene of nature; there is no time when it is not the revelation of heaven's mechanism. How then can a man be other than true? If a man's heart is not true, he has no true intent; with no true intent, he has no true feeling.

I have often seen men who cultivate the Way: in movement, private thoughts rise up one after another, and the privateness of those thoughts is where the heart is not true; in stillness, desires follow one upon another, and to dwell in desire is where the heart is not true. If private thoughts and desires are not cut off, what one utters may be wholly without true intent, or half true and half false; and the moment of half true and half false is precisely the moment when heaven and man contend within one. This intent is a thing no feeling can conceal. To test the true Way, first test the true feeling; testing the true feeling, one may know whether the heart is true or not, whether the intent is true or not.

Therefore the way of cultivating truth must begin with intent. When the intent is sincere, the heart is sincere too, and the feeling that issues from the heart is sincere as well. Sincerity — that is truth. If sincerity is not true, then when it appears in speech, the words do not come from the heart, and they are not true words. When it appears in action, the action does not follow one's nature, and it is not true action. He who cultivates must cultivate away the heart outside the heart, the intent outside the intent, the feeling outside the feeling. When a thought is raised or a word is spoken, one should lift up the heaven-given conscience and put down the human heart, and allow no doubting or dividing of the heart, no mixing and jumbling of the intent: only then are they true heart, true intent and true feeling, without a hair of falsehood, and this is the true Way. The true Way pervades all things; therefore it is called Complete Reality.”

When the Ancestor Lü had finished expounding the principle of Complete Reality to Wang the Filial and Incorrupt, he further transmitted to him all the labors of refining the self and laying the foundation, setting up the furnace and establishing the cauldron, gathering the medicine and returning the elixir, and the firing process of withdrawing and adding. The Filial and Incorrupt bowed twice and received the teaching. The Ancestor Lü also said, “After you have accomplished the Way, go quickly to Shandong to save the Seven Perfected. The Seven Perfected are the masters of the seven golden lotuses of which I spoke to you before.” When the Ancestor Lü had finished his injunctions, he and the Ancient Ancestor Zhongli gave themselves a leap, and golden light spread over all the ground, and in an instant they were gone. The Filial and Incorrupt bowed toward the empty sky in thanks; and when he had bowed, he still gazed up into the air, pondering in silence on the immortals' countenances.

He saw Wang Mao and Yuwa come up, saying, “We come by our mistress's command to look for our master. We suspected he would be here, and now indeed we have found him.” So they begged him to come home, that they might not be left anxious. The Filial and Incorrupt walked slowly, silently committing to memory all along the road the Way that the Ancestor Lü had transmitted.

When he reached home he did not go into the inner rooms, but went straight to the study and sat down. When Madam Zhou heard that her husband had come home she came at once to inquire after him, and saw the Filial and Incorrupt silent and unspeaking, looking as if his thoughts were elsewhere. When she had looked at him a while she urged her husband, saying, “You have again and again gone out lightly, and it always leaves me anxious; I fear only that it may stain your character and make you a laughing-stock among the villagers. You will not listen to my advice, time after time; what is to be done?” The Filial and Incorrupt was just then silently pondering the mysterious work, and he did not even know that Madam Zhou had come in, much less hear what she said. Only at the last, hearing her say suddenly, “What is to be done?” did he, unable to make head or tail of it, answer offhand, “What do you mean, what is to be done, and what is not to be done?” Seeing that his words made no sense, she said no more and went away.

The Filial and Incorrupt thought to himself, “With such disturbance as this, how can a man ever succeed or awaken to the Way? If I do not think of some device to cut off the ties of the dust, I shall never in this life be freed.” He bowed his head and thought a while, and thought out a way: unless he feigned a stroke and lost his speech, he could not cut off these entanglements. Having thought it out, he at once put on the manner of a dotard. When anyone came he made a show of groaning, and he would not go back to the inner rooms, but lay down on the cool couch in the study. When Madam Zhou saw this she was beside herself with worry, and came to ask after him several times a day. She saw him mumbling and muttering, his speech unclear, moaning and calling out and wagging his head without cease. There was nothing Madam Zhou could do; so she sent Yuwa to invite several of his old close friends to come and chat with him and see what the trouble might be.

These few friends were all men whom Wang the Filial and Incorrupt had always respected and loved. They came as soon as they were invited, and when they had entered the study they asked with one voice, “Is the Master Filial and Incorrupt well?” The Filial and Incorrupt shook his head several times and waved his hand several times, and in his mouth there was a babbling and sputtering; he could not speak, but only sighed. When the friends saw that he could not speak and did nothing but groan, they knew he was ill, but did not know what illness he had. One of the older men said, “To my eye the Master Filial and Incorrupt looks like a case of stroke with loss of speech. I do not know whether I am right. At the east end of our village there is a Mr. Zhang Haiqing, a physician of discernment. We could send someone to invite him to come and feel the pulse, and then we shall know the truth of it.”

Madam Zhou, hearing these words outside the door, at once told Yuwa to go and invite the physician. In no long time the physician was brought. All the friends rose to their feet and let the physician come in and sit down, and they explained to him the circumstances of the Filial and Incorrupt's condition. Zhang Haiqing then came to feel Wang the Filial and Incorrupt's pulse; when he had felt both wrists, there was no pulse of illness at all. He had no choice but to follow the tone of the company and say, “It is indeed a case of stroke with loss of speech; he need only take a few more doses of medicine, and I guarantee he will be cured.” With that he took up his brush and wrote out a few ingredients. Whether he could cure him or not, hear the next chapter's unfolding.
Not that the doctor's art was dim; / the graduate had no ailment in him.

blocks.text: 3. Receiving Heaven's Edict, He Saves the World in Shandong; Entering the Earth, He Hides at Zhongnan

inline.s: The world's warm-cold is past compare; / for fame and gain men strive and tear;
Living beings are easy to save, but man is hard; / I would save living beings, and man disregard.

The story tells that Wang the Filial and Incorrupt was in fact a man without illness; he had only feigned illness, wishing to cut off all entanglements so that he might awaken to the mysterious work. How could this Mr. Zhang Haiqing know the depth of his heart? So he felt the pulse on this side and on that, and could find no illness in him, and had no choice but to follow the tone of the company and say, “It is truly a case of stroke with loss of speech.” He at once asked for paper and brush and wrote out a prescription — nothing more than three qián of chuānxiōng and half a liǎng of fángfēng. When he had written it, he exchanged a few idle words with the company, drank a cup of fragrant tea, and then, having received his fee of thanks, went his way. After the physician had gone, the friends also took their leave of the military graduate Wang, saying, “Master Filial and Incorrupt, take good care of yourself; we are going home, and will come again another day to see you.” The military graduate Wang nodded his head a little, and the friends went off, each his own way.

When Madam Zhou saw the guests out, she called her son Qiulang and Yuwa to go to the medicine shop in the west village and bring back the medicine. They brewed it in a jar and poured it into a bowl, and made Qiulang carry it in both hands into the study. No sooner had he called out, “Papa, take your medicine,” than he saw his father open both eyes wide and stamp his foot fiercely; Qiulang was so frightened that he set the bowl down in a hurry and ran out, and the second time he was sent he would not come again. After Qiulang had gone, Wang the Filial and Incorrupt quietly poured the medicine away in a secluded spot. From that time on, only Yuwa came and went, bringing tea and handing water. As for the maids and serving-women, they dared not come before his door; if he saw them he would beat his breast and stamp his feet, and so none of them dared come. Even Madam Zhou, mindful of the love between husband and wife, came in to see him, and he would not have it. After he feigned the stroke, all affairs within and without were managed by his wife alone, and she had no leisure to come often and ask after him. Kinsmen and friends who came to visit him twice, seeing him in such a state, came no more. And so everyone said, “What a fine military graduate Wang, and a pity that he has fallen into a bad disease.” That one saying set him aside in a cold and lonely place, quiet and still, alone in his study, awakening to the Way and cultivating truth, practicing and sitting in meditation. Thus for twelve years, until his great elixir was accomplished.
His wife his comrade, his son his peer; / tea for his thirst, and rice his cheer;
He looked like any other man; / who knew that he was working out the Way's own plan?
Twelve years done, his merit crowned; / his yang spirit rose from his crown unbound;
How many cultivators there are in the world, and who among them could be willing to do the same

Now Wang the military graduate had cultivated the great Way at home and could send forth his yang spirit, dividing his body and transforming at will, and he gave himself a Daoist name, calling himself “Chongyang.” One night as this Wang Chongyang sat in meditation in the study, at the very moment when not a single thought arose and all sounds were still, he suddenly heard a voice call in the empty air, “Wang Chongyang, come quickly up to the clouds and receive the edict.” The voice pierced his ear. Chongyang hurriedly sprang up into the void, and saw the Great White Star standing upon the clouds, announcing that a jade edict had come down. Wang Chongyang knelt to hear it read. The edict said:

Considering that you, Chongyang, have with bitter resolve cultivated the Way for twelve years without the least fault, so that your fruit of the Way is now complete, We specially enfeoff you as the Zhenren of Opening Transformation. Go quickly to Shandong to save the world, and cause the Seven Perfected to ascend before long. When your merit is accomplished, further titles shall be added. Be reverent.” When the Golden Star had finished reading the edict, Chongyang bowed twice to thank the grace, and then exchanged courtesies with the Lord of the Great White Star. The Lord Star said, “Zhenren, go quickly to Shandong to save the world; do not fear hardship and weariness, and fail the Emperor's heart. When we meet another day at the Peach Banquet at the Jade Pond, we shall talk again.” Having spoken, the Lord Star returned of himself to the heavenly palace, and Chongyang went back to the study and sat in meditation.

That morning Yuwa brought water for him to wash his face, but could not push the door open, and hurried to tell the mistress of the house. Madam Zhou came with two maids to the door of the study, and called out in every way, but the door would not open. Thinking that the Filial and Incorrupt must be dead, they forced the door off its hinges and went in, and there was no one to be seen. Madam Zhou was alarmed and frightened, and hastily ordered people to search in all directions, but there was no trace of him at all. Madam Zhou wept aloud, and the whole village was roused and came to ask what had happened. Yuwa told the villagers the whole story, and they all said, “This is strange indeed: the door was bolted, and the man is gone. Could he have gone up over the roof or over the wall?” So they went in to look, and not a brick or a tile had been moved. They searched again by several roads, but there was no sign of him. Among them there was a man of some understanding who said, “There is no need for you to go looking. From the look of Wang the Filial and Incorrupt, I would say he has certainly become an immortal.” The villagers all asked, “How do you make out that he has become an immortal?” The man said, “He sat in this study for twelve years without moving a single step, pretending to have a stroke when in truth he was cutting himself off from the dust. I have often seen his face glowing red, and the spirit-light in his eyes piercing one through; had he not been an immortal, how could he have been like that?” When the people heard this they were half convinced and half doubtful, and said with one voice, “By this account he has certainly become an immortal and gone up to heaven on the clouds.” When Madam Zhou heard it, her grief was somewhat abated, and the people dispersed, each to his own home.

It is further told that on that day Wang Chongyang left Great Wei Village by the art of earth-soaring and came toward Shandong. He traveled several thousand li, but there was no sign of any Seven Perfected; he met only two kinds of men. And which two kinds? One was the man of “fame,” and one was the man of “profit.” Apart from these two sorts, there is no other kind of person. When Wang Chongyang saw that there was no one to save, he went back again to Shaanxi. When he came to the foot of Zhongnan, he saw a bare hill stretching a hundred li, so quiet and lovely that he thought it better to use a method of mastering earth and sink into the depths of the soil, lying hidden and buried there, and wait until a man who cultivates the Way should appear in the world; then he would come out and save him, and it would not be too late. So he twined his fingers in a mudra and recited a spell, and sank into the earth. In about the space of half a double-hour he had reached a place of the utmost depth, where there was a cavity that could quite contain his body. He entered the cavity and, in the manner of a creature that hibernates in winter (
zhé
, when an animal sleeps through the winter, hiding away and neither eating nor moving), he took in breath and regulated his breathing to preserve his life.
So vast a heaven and earth, and only two men; / one fame, one gain, turning the wheel again;
The Seven Perfected he could not find to save; / in earth he hid, awaiting what fate gave.

Now while Wang Chongyang lay hidden in the earth, he knew nothing of day or sky. It seemed that nearly half a year had passed when suddenly he heard a great crash, like the sky falling and the earth splitting, which shook open a crack in the earthen cavity and let in the light, and above there was a flashing of golden light. He knew that his venerable master had arrived. Wang Chongyang was greatly startled, and in a flurry he sprang up through the crack in the earth, and indeed he saw the two immortals Zhongli and Lü sitting together on an earthen platform. Wang Chongyang prostrated himself on the ground, not daring to look up. The Ancestor Lü laughed and said, “Other men cultivate the Way and go up to heaven; you now cultivate the Way and go down into the underworld. It seems your course of practice is quite different from other men's: you defy heaven above and go against your master's will below — is there such an immortal as this?” Chongyang bowed his head and confessed his fault, saying, “It is not that your disciple dared to defy heaven's will and go against my master's teaching; the truth is that in Shandong today there is no one to be saved, and so I hid myself for a time, to wait until a man who cultivates the Way should appear in the world, and then go and save him, without haste.”

The Ancestor Lü said, “Where is there a place without men who cultivate the Way? It is only that you are unwilling to take pains to seek and observe them, and so you cannot find them. Take yourself, for instance: at the first you had no mind at all to learn the Way. Had I, your patriarch, not come again and again to point you toward it, your whole life would have been no more than that of a Filial and Incorrupt; how could you ever have become a golden immortal of the Great Luo heaven? Now you crave only your own ease and will not press forward, and then you say there is no one in the world — is that not absurd? If you will take the method by which I saved you and use it in turn to save others, then there is no one in the world who cannot be saved. Of old I was three times drunk at Yueyang and no man knew me, and lightly I flew across Lake Dongting, thinking that there was none in the world worth saving. But when I went north again to Liaoyang and saw that the chancellor of the Jin state had the makings of one who could be saved, I pointed the way to him myself, and the chancellor at once gave up his seal and returned to the mountains, cultivated the great Way to completion, and called himself Haichan. Liu Haichan, following my example, journeyed south, and he in turn saved Zhang Ziyang; Zhang Ziyang saved Shi Xinglin; Shi Xinglin saved Xue Daoguang; Xue Daoguang saved Chen Zhixu; Chen Zhixu saved Bai Ziqing; and Bai Ziqing saved Liu Yongnian and Peng Helin. All seven of these men realized the fruit, and they are the Southern Seven Perfected. At that time I thought there was no one to be saved, and yet, as it turned out, I saved a great many. The world is vast, the four seas are broad, the wondrous principle is inexhaustible, and men of the utmost are not few; how can there be any principle that no one is to be saved? Now there are the Northern Seven Perfected: Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, Wang, and Sun. I have urged you again and again, yet you will not go to save them — is it that your power falls short of Haichan's? It is not that it falls short; it is because of your fear of difficulty, and that is why it falls short.”

When the Ancestor Lü had finished speaking, Chongyang's understanding was suddenly opened; he was frightened and confessed his fault, the sweat streaming down his back. The Ancient Ancestor Zhongli told him to rise and stand beside them, and said to him, “It is not that your master has urged you again and again for nothing. It is only that the time of the Peach Banquet is near at hand, when an edict will be sent to all the true immortals under heaven who have cultivated the Way and completed it, to come together to this feast. This peach grows on Mount Kunlun: a thousand years to flower, a thousand years to set its fruit, a thousand years to ripen — three thousand years in all before it is complete. The peach is as big as a bushel basket, red as a blazing fire; eat one and you live a thousand years. The Queen Mother of the West could not bear to enjoy it alone, and wished to share it with all the immortals, buddhas, gods and sages under heaven; so she established a feast called the Great Assembly of the Host of Immortals. At each feast there must be some newly accomplished immortals, and only then does the feast have luster. If there were only the old immortals and true men of former times, then it would be said that there are no men under heaven who cultivate the Way and learn the truth, and the Queen Mother would be displeased. In high antiquity each feast gained more than a thousand newly advanced true immortals; in middle antiquity each feast gained several hundred; but in this degenerate age, by reckoning, there will not be many. Therefore we charge you to save the Seven Perfected early, that they may go together to the Peach Banquet and add majesty and luster to the gathering. At present the peaches are about to ripen; if you delay and let this opportunity slip, you must wait another three thousand years before you can go to the feast. Would that not be a grievous pity?”

These words were spoken through and through, leaving nothing unclear. Zhenren Chongyang knelt again and said, “Your disciple, hearing today the words of the patriarch, is like one waking from a dream. Now I am willing to go again to Shandong to save and transform, and I beg the patriarch to point out the road ahead.” The Ancient Ancestor Zhongli said, “The land is crowded and men are thick; you must go among the crowded places of men, mingle your traces with the dust, and manifest your body to preach the Dharma. Of themselves men will come to seek you, and you may guide them from within, and the great work can be accomplished. On this journey: where you meet the sea, stay; where you meet Ma, flourish; where you meet Qiu, stop.” When the Ancient Ancestor Zhongli had finished speaking, he went off with the Ancestor Lü, riding on the clouds. Wang Chongyang came once more toward Shandong. One day he came to a county called Ninghai, which is under the jurisdiction of Dengzhou prefecture in Shandong. Zhenren Chongyang recalled the patriarch's words — “where you meet the sea, stay” — could it be that it was to be fulfilled in this place? So he stayed in that place, carrying an iron pot in his hand and using begging as his pretext, after the manner in which the Ancestor Lü had once saved him, in order to save others. Whether he could save them or not, see the next chapter's unfolding.
